headline: A billion-hectare bet: why nature's recovery hinges on quadrupling funding
meta_description: 252 million hectares are under restoration globally, but reaching 1 billion hectares by 2030 requires annual funding to jump from $64B to $296B—creating 32 mil…
summary_short: Nature restoration is accelerating across 149 countries, but the UN warns that funding must quadruple to meet ambitious 2030 targets and prevent species extinction.
body:
At the midpoint of the UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration, a remarkable milestone has been reached: some 252 million hectares of land and sea across 149 countries—roughly the size of Kazakhstan—are currently under restoration, the largest documented effort of its kind. This unprecedented scale has already created more than one million green jobs. Yet the real test lies ahead. To meet the global commitment of restoring one billion hectares by 2030 and safeguarding 30 percent of the world's ecosystems, annual restoration funding must leap from $64 billion to $296 billion. That investment could generate up to 32 million jobs worldwide over the next six years, transforming economic opportunity alongside ecological recovery.

The urgency is clear: research shows that restoring just 15 percent of global priority areas could prevent 60 percent of projected species extinctions while sequestering 30 percent of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions. Yet progress remains uneven. Terrestrial ecosystem restoration has reached nearly half its 30 percent target, while marine and coastal restoration lags significantly behind. Freshwater ecosystems, too, demand rapid acceleration. The challenge extends beyond money alone. Restoration must address the underlying drivers of ecosystem degradation and be sustained long enough to deliver lasting benefits to communities—work that demands both government investment in monitoring and a commitment to stop destroying while attempting to restore.
quick_facts: 252 million hectares under restoration across 149 countries as of now
Funding must grow from $64 billion to $296 billion annually by 2030
Could prevent 60% of projected species extinctions if 15% of priority areas restored
32 million green jobs possible worldwide by 2030 from restoration work
1 million green jobs already created during current restoration efforts
